claim: A knock-in mouse lacking the CTD of GluA1 expresses normal LTP.
source: We found that a knock-in mouse lacking the CTD of GluA1 expresses normal LTP and spatial memory, assayed by the Morris water maze.
evidence: The abstract directly states the main finding that the knock-in mouse shows normal LTP, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A knock-in mouse lacking the CTD of GluA1 expresses normal spatial memory as assayed by the Morris water maze.
source: We found that a knock-in mouse lacking the CTD of GluA1 expresses normal LTP and spatial memory, assayed by the Morris water maze.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by behavioral data from Morris water maze experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: LTP generates synaptic slots which capture passively diffusing AMPARs.
source: Our results support a model in which LTP generates synaptic slots, which capture passively diffusing AMPARs.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings, representing an interpretation of the data.

claim: LTP requires the activity-dependent trafficking of AMPA receptors to the synapse.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) requires the activity-dependent trafficking of AMPA receptors (AMPARs) to the synapse (Collingridge et al., 2004; Malinow and Malenka, 2002; Nicoll, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this requirement.

claim: Most AMPARs in CA1 pyramidal cells are heterotetramers of either GluA1/GluA2 subunits or GluA2/GluA3 subunits.
source: Most AMPARs in CA1 pyramidal cells are heterotetramers of either GluA1/GluA2 subunits or GluA2/GluA3 subunits, although other complexes can also occur (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: The prevailing LTP model posits that LTP-mediated covalent modification of the intracellular carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of GluA1 results in the capture of these modified GluA1 containing receptors by preexisting 'slots' in the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: The prevailing, receptor centric, LTP model, posits that LTP-mediated covalent modification of the intracellular carboxy-terminal domain (CTD, also referred to as C-tail) of GluA1 results in the capture of these modified GluA1 containing receptors by preexisting 'slots' in the postsynaptic density (PSD) (Hayashi et al., 2000; Huganir and Nicoll, 2013; Malinow and Malenka, 2002; Shi et al., 2001), either by increasing the surface pool of AMPARs or the docking of AMPAR at the PSD.
evidence: This describes a prevailing model in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two phosphorylation sites in the GluA1 CTD, S831 and S845, have received most of the attention.
source: Two phosphorylation sites in the GluA1 CTD, S831 and S845, have received most of the attention.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of research in the field.

claim: The occurrence of S831 and S845 phosphorylation in vivo is a matter of debate.
source: However, the occurrence of S831 and S845 phosphorylation in vivo is a matter of debate.
evidence: This acknowledges ongoing scientific debate about these phosphorylation sites.

claim: A recent study found the relative abundance of phosphorylated GluA1 to be 'almost negligible'.
source: A recent study found the relative abundance of phosphorylated GluA1 to be 'almost negligible' (Hosokawa et al., 2015), but see Diering et al., 2016.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hosokawa et al., 2015.

claim: The replacement by alanine of either S831 or S845 does not affect LTP.
source: The replacement by alanine of either of these residues does not affect LTP (Lee et al., 2010), and only adult double phosphomutant mice have partially impaired LTP (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Only adult double phosphomutant mice (S831A and S845A) have partially impaired LTP.
source: The replacement by alanine of either of these residues does not affect LTP (Lee et al., 2010), and only adult double phosphomutant mice have partially impaired LTP (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: A previous study expressed a heteromeric receptor containing the GluA1 subunit lacking the CTD (GluA1ΔC) as well as GluA2, and observed normal basal trafficking and LTP at CA1 synapses in acute hippocampal slices.
source: In the most relevant experiment in our study, we expressed a heteromeric receptor containing the GluA1 subunit lacking the CTD (GluA1ΔC) as well as GluA2, and observed normal basal trafficking and LTP at CA1 synapses in acute hippocampal slices.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors (Granger et al., 2013) describing experimental findings.

claim: AMPAR lacking the GluA1 subunit CTD can traffic normally to the synapse and enable normal LTP.
source: We therefore concluded that AMPAR lacking the GluA1 subunit CTD can traffic normally to the synapse and enable normal LTP (Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Zhou et al. generated a knock-in mouse in which they replaced the endogenous GluA1 with a chimeric GluA1 subunit that contains the CTD of GluA2 (GluA1A2CTD).
source: The authors generated a knock-in (KI) mouse, in which they replaced the endogenous GluA1 with a chimeric GluA1 subunit that contains the CTD of GluA2 (GluA1A2CTD).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Zhou et al. found that while basal synaptic transmission was normal in the GluA1A2CTD mouse, LTP was absent.
source: They found that, while basal synaptic transmission was normal in this mouse, LTP was absent.
evidence: This describes findings from Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: A complementary chimeric AMPAR subunit, GluA2A1CTD, fully rescued LTP in the Zhou et al. study.
source: Furthermore, a complementary chimeric AMPAR subunit, GluA2A1CTD, fully rescued LTP.
evidence: This describes findings from Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Zhou et al. concluded that the CTD of GluA1 is 'necessary and sufficient' for NMDAR dependent LTP.
source: Thus, the authors concluded that the CTD of GluA1 is 'necessary and sufficient' for NMDAR dependent LTP.
evidence: This describes the conclusion of Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Replacement of endogenous GluA2 subunits with GluA1/A2CTD resulted in functional AMPARs which supported homeostatic synaptic scaling.
source: We previously showed that replacement of endogenous GluA2 subunits with GluA1/A2CTD resulted in functional AMPARs, which supported homeostatic synaptic scaling (Ancona Esselmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of GluA1/A2CTD in hippocampal slice cultures generated rectifying synaptic responses.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of this construct in hippocampal slice cultures generated rectifying synaptic responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), confirming that this construct forms functional homomeric receptors which traffic to the synapse constitutively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GluA1/A2CTD forms functional homomeric receptors which traffic to the synapse constitutively.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of this construct in hippocampal slice cultures generated rectifying synaptic responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), confirming that this construct forms functional homomeric receptors which traffic to the synapse constitutively.
evidence: This is inferred from the rectifying synaptic responses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Synaptic AMPARs were fully rescued when all endogenous AMPARs were replaced with heteromeric GluA1/A2CTD-GluA2(R) receptors in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Synaptic AMPARs were fully rescued (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Synaptic currents were non-rectifying in GluA1/A2CTD-GluA2(R) expressing neurons, confirming that the expressed subunits form heteromeric receptors.
source: Unlike replacement with GluA1/A2CTD alone, which results in strongly rectifying, homomeric AMPARs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), synaptic currents were non-rectifying in GluA1/A2CTD-GluA2(R) expressing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), confirming that the expressed subunits form heteromeric receptors.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: GluA1/A2CTD-GluA2(R) heteromeric receptors exhibit normal LTP.
source: These receptors exhibit normal LTP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Co-transfection of a Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 expressing vector in cells expressing GluA1 virtually eliminated the GluA1 protein.
source: Co-transfection of a Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 expressing vector in cells expressing GluA1 virtually eliminated the GluA1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Expression of the Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 in rat slice cultures and mouse acute slices resulted in a ~50% loss of AMPAR EPSCs.
source: Similar to the results obtained using the conditional KO of GluA1 using Cre-loxP (Granger et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2009), we observed a ~50% loss of AMPAR EPSCs when expressing the Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 in rat slice cultures and mouse acute slices (therefore, data were pooled, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: NMDAR EPSCs remained unchanged after Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 expression.
source: NMDAR EPSCs remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: LTP was absent after Gria1 gRNA/Cas9 expression, likely due to the lack of a sufficient reserve pool of receptors.
source: LTP was absent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), in agreement with previous results, likely due to the lack of a sufficient reserve pool of receptors (Granger et al., 2013; Zamanillo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and citations to previous work.

claim: GluA1/A2CTD* expression rescued basal synaptic transmission after endogenous GluA1 deletion.
source: GluA1/A2CTD* expression rescued basal synaptic transmission (Figure 1E) and LTP (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GluA1/A2CTD* expression rescued LTP after endogenous GluA1 deletion.
source: GluA1/A2CTD* expression rescued basal synaptic transmission (Figure 1E) and LTP (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: NMDAR EPSCs were normal in transfected cells expressing GluA1/A2CTD*.
source: NMDAR EPSCs were normal in transfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The HA tag is present in both the heterozygous and the homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice, but is absent from WT mice.
source: The HA tag, which we attached to the truncated C-terminus to identify the ΔCTD GluA1 subunit, is present in both the heterozygous and the homozygous KI mice, but, as expected, is absent from WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CTD directed antibody labeled the WT and heterozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice, but not the homozygous KI mouse.
source: The CTD directed antibody labeled the WT and heterozygous, but not the homozygous KI mouse.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ATD-directed antibody demonstrated the presence of GluA1 at normal levels in the HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mouse, where the protein size is reduced due to the lack of the C-terminal 77 amino acids.
source: The ATD-directed antibody demonstrated the presence of GluA1 at normal levels in the KI mouse, where, as expected, the protein size is reduced due to the lack of the C-terminal 77 amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunoblot against the GluA2 CTD and NR1 showed normal levels of these synaptic proteins in the HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mouse.
source: Immunoblot against the GluA2 CTD and NR1 showed normal levels of these synaptic proteins in the KI (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence using a GluA1 CTD antibody yielded strong staining in the WT hippocampal CA1 region, but no staining in the HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mouse.
source: Truncation of the GluA1 CTD was further confirmed with immunofluorescence using a GluA1 CTD antibody, which yielded strong staining in the WT hippocampal CA1 region, but no staining in the KI mouse (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AMPAR responses recorded from somatic outside out patches were unchanged in the HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mouse.
source: AMPAR responses recorded from somatic outside out patches were unchanged in the KI mouse (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LTP expression is critically dependent on the level of extrasynaptic AMPARs.
source: This is particularly important, because LTP expression is critically dependent on the level of extrasynaptic AMPARs (Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Granger et al., 2013.

claim: There was no change in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio in the HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mouse, consistent with a normal number of synaptic AMPARs.
source: Furthermore, there was no change in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio, consistent with a normal number of synaptic AMPARs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Pairing-induced LTP (2 Hz/90 s. stimuli, while holding the postsynaptic neuron at 0 mV) in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice was no different from WT controls.
source: Pairing-induced LTP (2 Hz/90 s. stimuli, while holding the postsynaptic neuron at 0 mV) in these KI mice was no different from WT controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: LTP induced with a different pairing protocol (two stimulus bouts of 100 Hz/1 s. while holding the postsynaptic neuron at 0 mV) showed no impairment in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice.
source: To obtain an independent analysis of these mice, we collaborated with another group (R.C. Malenka and W. Morishita, Stanford University) who induced LTP with a different pairing protocol consisting of two stimulus bouts of 100 Hz/1 s. while holding the postsynaptic neuron at 0 mV. Again, no impairment in LTP was observed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No statistically significant difference between WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice was found in the distance travelled to find the hidden platform during Morris water maze training.
source: No statistically significant difference between WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice was found in either the distance travelled to find the hidden platform during training (Figure 3A), or in the ability to remember the position of the platform 24 hr after the last training session (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No statistically significant difference between WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice was found in the ability to remember the position of the platform 24 hr after the last training session in the Morris water maze.
source: No statistically significant difference between WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice was found in either the distance travelled to find the hidden platform during training (Figure 3A), or in the ability to remember the position of the platform 24 hr after the last training session (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice showed a reduced swim speed across the training and test sessions in the Morris water maze.
source: HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice showed a reduced swim speed across the training and test sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E), which increased their latency to find the platform during training (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and resulted in a not significant trend toward increased latency to the first platform crossing in the probe trial (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: Reduced swim speed in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice increased their latency to find the platform during Morris water maze training.
source: HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice showed a reduced swim speed across the training and test sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E), which increased their latency to find the platform during training (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and resulted in a not significant trend toward increased latency to the first platform crossing in the probe trial (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice showed a not significant trend toward increased latency to the first platform crossing in the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice showed a reduced swim speed across the training and test sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E), which increased their latency to find the platform during training (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and resulted in a not significant trend toward increased latency to the first platform crossing in the probe trial (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GluA1 KO mice show no spatial learning defects in the Morris water maze.
source: Given that GluA1 KO mice show no spatial learning defects in the Morris water maze (Zamanillo et al., 1999), it is not surprising that mice lacking the GluA1 CTD did not show a spatial learning impairment in our study either.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zamanillo et al., 1999.

claim: The severe deficits found in spatial learning and memory in GluA1/A2CTD KI mice by Zhou et al. are puzzling.
source: The severe deficits found in spatial learning and memory in GluA1/A2CTD KI mice are, therefore, puzzling.
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors comparing their results to those of Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Both GluA1 KO and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice show decreased swim speed compared to their WT controls.
source: Of note, both GluA1 KO (Zamanillo et al., 1999) and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E) mice show decreased swim speed compared to their WT controls, a possible confounding factor suggesting that the GluA1 CTD might be involved in this locomotor function.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E and citation to Zamanillo et al., 1999.

claim: The GluA1 CTD might be involved in locomotor function.
source: Of note, both GluA1 KO (Zamanillo et al., 1999) and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,E) mice show decreased swim speed compared to their WT controls, a possible confounding factor suggesting that the GluA1 CTD might be involved in this locomotor function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed swim speed differences.

claim: Posttranslational modifications targeting the GluA1 CTD are involved in the modulation of AMPAR synaptic transmission, LTP and spatial memory.
source: Although we failed to find a fundamental requirement for the GluA1 CTD in AMPAR synaptic transmission, LTP and spatial memory, it has previously been shown that posttranslational modifications targeting this domain are involved in the modulation of these phenomena, particularly LTP.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research in the field.

claim: Phosphorylation of GluA1 C-tail residues S831 and S845 is well-established.
source: Perhaps, the well-established phosphorylation of GluA1 C-tail residues (particularly S831 and S845) (Barria et al., 1997; Esteban et al., 2003; Hayashi et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Mammen et al., 1997; Roche et al., 1996) is crucial to relieve some, yet unidentified, negative modulatory effect exerted by other part(s) of the GluA1 C-tail, this negative modulation being absent in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice and in cells expressing GluA1/A2CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of S831 and S845 might be crucial to relieve some unidentified negative modulatory effect exerted by other part(s) of the GluA1 C-tail.
source: Perhaps, the well-established phosphorylation of GluA1 C-tail residues (particularly S831 and S845) (Barria et al., 1997; Esteban et al., 2003; Hayashi et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Mammen et al., 1997; Roche et al., 1996) is crucial to relieve some, yet unidentified, negative modulatory effect exerted by other part(s) of the GluA1 C-tail, this negative modulation being absent in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice and in cells expressing GluA1/A2CTD.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: LTP does not require the GluA1 CTD.
source: Our data indicate that LTP does not require the GluA1 CTD and is, therefore, consistent with a model where LTP can occur independently of the subunit composition of AMPAR, in agreement with a previous study (Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LTP can occur independently of the subunit composition of AMPAR.
source: Our data indicate that LTP does not require the GluA1 CTD and is, therefore, consistent with a model where LTP can occur independently of the subunit composition of AMPAR, in agreement with a previous study (Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citation to Granger et al., 2013.

claim: The 'PSD centric model' for LTP proposes that the LTP signal creates/unmasks new slots in the PSD that capture passively diffusing, unmodified AMPARs.
source: More broadly, our results suggest an alternative model, which we refer to as the 'PSD centric model' for LTP, in which the LTP signal creates/unmasks new slots in the PSD that capture passively diffusing, unmodified AMPARs.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Constitutive and activity-dependent AMPAR trafficking has two essential requirements: the multivalent interaction between transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins (TARPs) and PSD scaffolding proteins (the intracellular slot), and the presence of the GluA1 amino-terminal domain and its interaction with yet to be identified extracellular synaptic cleft moieties (the extracellular slot).
source: Based on recent findings from us and others (Díaz-Alonso et al., 2017; Sheng et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2019), we propose that constitutive and activity-dependent AMPAR trafficking has two essential requirements. On one hand, the multivalent interaction between transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins (TARPs) and PSD scaffolding proteins (the intracellular slot). On the other hand, the presence of the GluA1 amino-terminal domain and its interaction with yet to be identified extracellular synaptic cleft moieties (the extracellular slot).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on recent findings, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The activity-regulated availability of both intracellular and extracellular slots can modulate the abundance of functional AMPARs at the synapse.
source: This emerging model predicts that the activity-regulated availability of both intracellular and extracellular slots can modulate the abundance of functional AMPARs at the synapse.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: The HA-ΔCTD GluA1 allele has the entire cytoplasmic tail truncated after the fourth amino acid after the last TM helix.
source: Schematic illustration of WT GluA1 (left) and transgenic HA-ΔCTD GluA1 (right). The latter has the entire cytoplasmic tail truncated after the fourth amino acid after the last TM helix.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Western blots show specific and allelic dose-dependent presence of haemmaglutinin (HA) tag only in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains.
source: Western blots showing specific and allelic dose-dependent presence of haemmaglutinin (HA) tag only in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, partial and total absence of signal from anti-GluA1 CTD antibody in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, respectively and decreased size of the GluA1 protein as a result of the truncation of the cytoplasmic tail in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Western blots show partial and total absence of signal from anti-GluA1 CTD antibody in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, respectively.
source: Western blots showing specific and allelic dose-dependent presence of haemmaglutinin (HA) tag only in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, partial and total absence of signal from anti-GluA1 CTD antibody in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, respectively and decreased size of the GluA1 protein as a result of the truncation of the cytoplasmic tail in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Western blots show decreased size of the GluA1 protein as a result of the truncation of the cytoplasmic tail in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains.
source: Western blots showing specific and allelic dose-dependent presence of haemmaglutinin (HA) tag only in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, partial and total absence of signal from anti-GluA1 CTD antibody in heterozygous and homozygous HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains, respectively and decreased size of the GluA1 protein as a result of the truncation of the cytoplasmic tail in HA-ΔCTD GluA1 mice brains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GluA2 CTD and NR1 signals did not differ substantially among genotypes in Western blots.
source: GluA2 CTD and NR1 signals did not differ substantially among genotypes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Overexpression of GluA1/A2CTD in hippocampal slice cultures results in strongly rectifying synaptic responses.
source: Synaptic rectification of AMPAR EPSCs measured in control and GluA1/A2CTD overexpressing CA1 pyramidal neurons 2–3 days after transfection in the presence of 0.1 mM AP5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Replacement of endogenous AMPAR with GluA1/A2CTD alone results in strongly rectifying, homomeric AMPARs.
source: Unlike replacement with GluA1/A2CTD alone, which results in strongly rectifying, homomeric AMPARs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), synaptic currents were non-rectifying in GluA1/A2CTD-GluA2(R) expressing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), confirming that the expressed subunits form heteromeric receptors.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both Gria1 crRNAs tested were able to disrupt the expression of overexpressed GluA1 in 293 T cells.
source: 2 crRNAs where tested to generate the KI mice. Both of them were able to disrupt the expression of overexpressed GluA1 in 293 T cells, so half of the oocytes were injected with each of them.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The distance necessary to find the platform in the Morris water maze decreased during training in both WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice.
source: Mixed effects analysis revealed that the distance necessary to find the platform decreased during training in both groups (day effect, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and described in the figure legend.

claim: There was a significant interaction between day and genotype in the Morris water maze training.
source: Although there was only a trend toward a genotype effect (p=0.0539), there was a significant interaction between day and genotype (p<0.05).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and described in the figure legend.

claim: Both WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice showed a clear preference for the target location vs non-target locations in the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: Both genotypes showed a clear preference for the target location vs non-target locations (WT, p=0.0010, KI, p=0.0012,).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the figure legend.

claim: WT and HA-ΔCTD GluA1 KI mice did not differ significantly in how many times they crossed the target location in the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: WT and KI mice did not differ significantly in how many times they crossed the target location (p=0.582 by Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the figure legend.

claim: Mixed effects analysis revealed a significant effect of genotype and day on swim speed during Morris water maze training.
source: Mixed effects analysis revealed a significant effect of genotype (p<0.01) and day (p<0.0001) during both the hidden and cued training but no significant genotype x day interaction for either training phase (p=0.455, hidden platform, p=0.722 cued platform).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: The time it took mice to find the platform in the Morris water maze decreased by day, with a clear effect of genotype but no significant day x genotype interaction.
source: Mixed effects analysis showed that the time it took mice to find the platform decreased by day (p<0.0001), with a clear effect of genotype (p<0.01) but no significant day x genotype interaction (p=0.205).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and described in the figure legend.

claim: Mice of either genotype showed a preference for the target quadrant vs the other quadrants in the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: Mice of either genotype showed a preference for the target quadrant vs the other quadrants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and described in the figure legend.
